extracted.intended_audience: NLP/AI researchers and policy analysts interested in automated policy-document analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of AI (LLM) systems on question-answering and content-extraction tasks applied to complex policy documents (case study: Executive Order 14110), comparing automated outputs to human expert analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of information extraction / question answering
rubrics_metrics.description: AI systems should provide accurate information extraction from complex policy documents and correctly answer representative policy questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study measured AI performance on question answering and content extraction tasks and compared it to manual analysis by human experts; accuracy is judged by correctness relative to human analysts and ground-truth interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability of outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: AI outputs should be reliable—consistent and trustworthy when extracting information from policy texts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract emphasizes 'accurate and reliable information extraction' as a success criterion for systems like Gemini 1.5 Pro and Claude 3 Opus; reliability is considered alongside accuracy when comparing to human analysts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency (speed and resource gains)
rubrics_metrics.description: AI systems should provide significant efficiency improvements over manual human analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper reports AI performed comparably to human analysts 'but with significantly higher efficiency'; efficiency is an explicit evaluation dimension (time/resource savings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative performance versus human experts
rubrics_metrics.description: AI system performance should be evaluated relative to manual analysis by human experts to determine practical parity or gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study directly compares four commercial AI systems to human analysts to assess whether AI can support or substitute parts of policy analysis workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility of AI analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Results produced by AI systems should be reproducible across runs, prompts, and system versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The abstract notes 'achieving reproducibility remains a challenge', highlighting reproducibility as a necessary criterion and an area needing further research and development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task coverage: question answering and content extraction suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems should be capable of handling the core task types required for policy analysis—question answering and content extraction—from long, complex documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The research focuses on these two task categories as representative of policy-analysis needs; successful systems should demonstrate competence on both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality across multiple commercial systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation should consider multiple AI systems to assess whether observed performance is system-specific or generalizable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This study used four commercial AI systems to analyze the document; comparing multiple systems helps identify which approaches consistently perform well (e.g., Gemini 1.5 Pro and Claude 3 Opus) and which do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of representative policy questions and realistic case study
rubrics_metrics.description: The evaluation should use a set of representative policy questions and a real-world policy document to ensure ecological validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper used Executive Order 14110 and 'a set of representative policy questions' as the testbed; constructing realistic questions and using an actual executive order increases relevance of findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of strengths and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond quantitative metrics, evaluations should identify strengths and limitations of AI approaches for policy analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The abstract states the study aimed 'to identify the strengths and limitations of current AI approaches', implying qualitative analysis of failure modes, boundary conditions, and practical considerations is part of a complete evaluation.
